name: chem-g2-r1
context:
GAME TWO OF THREE. Phase 0 and 1 of the build pattern, run before any design was drafted. Four measurements, THREE OF THEM NEGATIVE, and the negatives did more work than the positive.

─────────── WHAT I MEASURED BEFORE I DESIGNED ANYTHING ───────────

The chemistry engine already exists and is held by 20 oracles. Conservation of mass is a law in it: atoms in equals atoms out, nothing vanishes, nothing is conjured. Reactions score as a DIFFERENCE (bonds broken minus bonds formed), which an earlier measurement established is what makes size stop predicting score — assembling from free atoms had correlation(atom count, energy) = 0.843, and rearrangement dropped it to 0.122.

The engine also carries ΔG = ΔH − TΔS with T HARDCODED AT 298 K. That constant looked like the opening for a mechanic nothing else in the set has: let the player control temperature, and the available chemistry changes under them.

MEASUREMENT 1 — the option set really is temperature-sensitive. Over 53,410 rearrangements on 120 boards, 15.4% flip spontaneity somewhere between 200 K and 2500 K, and the flip is BIDIRECTIONAL: heating from 298 to 1800 unlocks 6,209 reactions and destroys 1,389. A real trade, not an upgrade.

MEASUREMENT 2 — AND IT KILLED THE MECHANIC. Does the BEST move change with temperature? Over 400 boards: 0.0%. Not one board. Mean energy gain from choosing the right temperature: 0.0%. The cause is structural — the highest-energy reaction is the biggest exotherm, a big exotherm has a large negative ΔH, and ΔG = ΔH − TΔS is therefore already negative at room temperature. Heating only ever unlocks reactions too weak to choose.

MEASUREMENT 3 — the obvious rescue also failed. If the objective were REACHING A TARGET rather than maximising energy, an endothermic step that only runs hot would become necessary. Over 16 targets × 60 boards at 298/800/1800 K: 0 of 16 targets became more reachable. Two got WORSE — H2O2 fell from 4 boards to 1, NH3 from 4 to 3 — which is the engine being right rather than broken, because hydrogen peroxide genuinely decomposes when heated.

So temperature is recorded as a FALSIFIED DESIGN DIRECTION. It is physically real in this engine and mechanically inert, and I would have built it on the strength of measurement 1 alone.

─────────── MEASUREMENT 4, WHICH IS THE GAME ───────────

The engine's own header names the thing I had been walking past: 'N₂ carries 941 kJ/mol, more than almost anything on the board, and is nearly useless as a reactant precisely because breaking that triple bond costs more than most rearrangements can repay. A big tile becomes a liability.'

That is a THERMODYNAMIC SINK. Hypothesis: greedy play manufactures sinks and destroys its own future. Measured over 250 boards, 12 turns, sinks = {N2, CO2, HF}:

    policy       banked   sinks at end   turns survived   options t1 -> t6 -> t12
    RANDOM         3067       13.6             11.9        299 -> 144 -> 37
    GREEDY         3771       15.0              9.5        299 ->  48 ->  1
    SINK-AWARE     3651       13.8             11.2        299 ->  87 -> 11

Boards start with 6.7 sinks of 36 cells. GREEDY MORE THAN DOUBLES THEM, runs out of legal moves two and a half turns before the game ends, and finishes with ONE option where random play has 37. It poisons the board it is standing on.

MEASUREMENT 5 — and the horizon does not rescue it either. Sweeping game length, the crossover where sink-aware play overtakes greedy is turn 20, and the margin there is 0.2%. Everything plateaus, because the board RUNS DRY at 9 to 14 turns whatever the policy. Conservation means the extractable energy is finite and the system winds down to equilibrium.

─────────── THE DESIGN THIS LEAVES ───────────

Not a match-3 with chemistry painted on. A CLOSED SYSTEM YOU ARE MANAGING THE DECLINE OF.

Farkle's question is 'again?'. Chemistry's is 'WHAT AM I DESTROYING?' — every reaction is practically irreversible, the greedy move strands atoms in bonds too strong to break, and the board's total extractable energy is a physical constant of the tiles you were dealt.

ENTROPY IS THE CLOCK. There is no turn limit worth having, because the board imposes its own: play ends when nothing exothermic remains. A player is not racing a timer, they are racing the system's decay toward equilibrium, and every move they make brings that end closer. That is thermodynamics as a game loop rather than as flavour text.

SCORE IS A FRACTION OF THE BOARD'S OWN CEILING, not an absolute. Two boards do not contain the same energy, so an absolute score would mostly measure the deal. A percentage of what THIS board could have given makes every deal comparable and makes the skill legible: you extracted 71% of what was there.

─────────── WHAT CARRIES OVER AND WHAT DOES NOT ───────────

CARRIES: conservation as a law; reactions scoring as a difference; the real bond-enthalpy and entropy tables; ΔG for spontaneity; the ported deterministic PRNG and persona population; the dual-constraint gate; one executor the server replays.

DOES NOT: the run multiplier (Farkle's answer to Farkle's problem); push-your-luck; the live hand; a turn cap; the forecast strip in its current form — a closed system's future is not a draw queue, it is the decay of what is already on the board.

─────────── WHAT IS NOT YET MEASURED ───────────

The board's physical ceiling and the headroom above a simple policy. A beam search for it is running and exceeded its first timeout, which is itself informative about how large the move space is. Until it lands I do not know whether skill has room above the greedy line, and that is the number that decides whether this is a game.

questions.text: I killed a temperature mechanic that was physically real in the engine because the best move never changed. Was that the right call, or does a mechanic that alters 15% of the option set have value I am not seeing by only looking at the chosen move?

The core is 'a closed system you manage the decline of', with entropy as the clock and no turn limit. Is a game whose board provably runs dry satisfying to play, or does it read as a game that breaks?
Scoring as a percentage of each board's own physical energy ceiling makes deals comparable. What does that scoring choice hide or distort?

Greedy banks 3771 and dies at turn 9.5; sink-aware banks 3651 and survives to 11.2. Right now the greedy player still wins on points. What is the most honest way to make foresight pay WITHOUT inventing a bonus that is not chemistry?
Name the strongest reason this design is less interesting than Farkle rather than differently interesting.
